value.overview: The Western Sandpiper is a small shorebird that breeds in western and northern Alaska and migrates along the Pacific Flyway to wintering areas from the southern United States through Central America and western South America. It is one of the most numerous shorebirds in North America and is especially associated with coastal mudflats and estuaries. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly as a migrant and winter visitor, where flocks may gather in productive tidal wetlands.
value.classification: The Western Sandpiper belongs to the sandpiper family, Scolopacidae, and the genus Calidris. Its scientific name is Calidris mauri.
value.identification: This small sandpiper has a short, slightly downcurved bill, black legs, and a compact body. Adults in breeding plumage show rusty, black, and brown markings on the head, breast, and back, while nonbreeding birds are mostly gray above and pale below. Juveniles often have crisp, scaly upperparts. The species can be difficult to distinguish from Semipalmated Sandpipers, but its subtly drooped bill, finer-tipped appearance, and typical flocking behavior can help with identification.
value.rangeHabitat: Western Sandpipers breed in tundra habitats in western and northern Alaska and migrate through coastal areas of western North America. They winter from the southern United States through Mexico and Central America to parts of northern South America. In Costa Rica, the species is recorded primarily along the Pacific coast, especially at tidal mudflats, estuaries, mangrove edges, salt ponds, and the Gulf of Nicoya. It may also use other shallow coastal wetlands during migration and the nonbreeding season.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Western Sandpipers pass through Costa Rica during migration and also winter there, with the largest concentrations generally associated with Pacific-coast tidal wetlands. Most individuals are absent from Costa Rica during the breeding season in northern summer.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in open Arctic and subarctic tundra, often near wet depressions, ponds, streams, or coastal areas. The nest is a shallow scrape on the ground, usually lined with small plant material. The female typically lays four eggs, and both adults may participate in incubation and care of the young. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves while adults provide protection. The species generally breeds during the short Arctic summer.
value.dietFeeding: Western Sandpipers feed mainly on small aquatic invertebrates, including insects, crustaceans, mollusks, and other tiny organisms. On tidal flats they probe soft mud with their bills and pick prey from the surface, often feeding rapidly in dense flocks as the tide changes. They may also consume seeds and other plant material. In Costa Rica, feeding is concentrated in exposed mudflats, estuaries, mangroves, and shallow coastal ponds.
value.behavior: This species is highly social outside the breeding season and commonly forms large, tightly coordinated flocks with other small shorebirds. It walks and runs across exposed mud while probing and picking at prey, and it frequently rests in compact groups above the high-tide line. During migration it undertakes long flights between stopover sites. Flocks can respond quickly to predators, rising together in swift, twisting formations before settling again in wetland habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although the species remains numerous and widely distributed.
conservation.threats: The main concerns are loss and degradation of coastal wetlands, disturbance at feeding and roosting sites, pollution, altered water regimes, and climate-related changes affecting Arctic breeding areas and migration stopovers. In Costa Rica, protection of Pacific-coast mudflats, estuaries, mangroves, and other tidal wetlands is particularly important.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore coastal wetlands used by shorebirds, maintain natural tidal flows, reduce pollution, and limit disturbance near feeding and high-tide roosting areas. In Costa Rica, visitors should keep dogs leashed, avoid flushing large shorebird flocks, respect protected-area rules, and support monitoring and conservation of important Pacific-coast wetlands.
